raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart-failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, without another identifiable cause and with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), usually <45% [1,2]. Modern definitions emphasize that PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion and a heterogeneous clinicopathological entity rather than a single disease [3,4]. Although uncommon, it is a leading cause of maternal cardiovascular morbidity and mortality because it affects young women, may present abruptly with pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock, and has implications for breastfeeding, anticoagulation, contraception, and future pregnancies [5,6].

Incidence varies strikingly by geography and ancestry. Population-based North American studies estimate roughly 1 case per 1,000–4,000 live births, with increasing recognition over time [7-9]. Black ancestry, older maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and lower socioeconomic status are consistent risk factors [8-10]. Global registry data show that women in Africa and parts of Asia often present later, with more severe heart failure and less access to guideline-directed therapy, contributing to worse outcomes [11]. These disparities suggest an interaction between genetic susceptibility, pregnancy-related vascular stress, environmental exposures, and health-system factors.

The pathobiology of PPCM links late gestation and puerperium to myocardial vulnerability. Earlier work identified inflammatory activation and oxidative stress as correlates of severity and recovery [12]. A pivotal experimental study showed that oxidative stress can activate cathepsin D, cleaving prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment with antiangiogenic, proapoptotic, and vasculotoxic effects [13]. A complementary model implicated impaired cardiac angiogenic signaling, with excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and reduced vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, providing a mechanistic bridge between pre-eclampsia and PPCM [14,15]. Familial clustering and sequencing studies have demonstrated overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy, especially truncating variants in TTN, supporting the concept that pregnancy may unmask latent genetic cardiomyopathy in some patients [16-18].

Clinically, PPCM resembles other causes of heart failure: dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, edema, fatigue, palpitations, chest discomfort, or syncope. Diagnosis is frequently delayed because normal pregnancy causes dyspnea, tachycardia, edema, and mild natriuretic peptide changes. Echocardiography is central, documenting LVEF reduction, chamber size, right ventricular function, mitral regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [19]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can help assess ventricular volumes, myocarditis mimics, scar, and thrombus, particularly postpartum when gadolinium is feasible [20]. Natriuretic peptides support the diagnosis and can aid follow-up; troponin elevation should prompt evaluation for ischemia, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, or hypertensive emergency. Differential diagnoses include pre-existing cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, acute coronary syndromes including spontaneous coronary artery dissection, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, thyroid disease, and amniotic-fluid embolism.

Prognosis is variable. In the North American IPAC cohort, most recovery occurred within 6 months, and baseline LVEF, left ventricular dilation, race, and clinical severity predicted outcomes [21]. Right ventricular dysfunction adds prognostic information and identifies women at higher risk of persistent dysfunction and adverse events [22]. Biomarker studies support the prognostic value of inflammatory, oxidative, prolactin-related, and angiogenic markers, although none replaces careful imaging and clinical follow-up [23]. Approximately half to two-thirds of women recover normal or near-normal LVEF, but persistent cardiomyopathy, thromboembolism, arrhythmia, transplantation, mechanical circulatory support, and death remain important risks.

Management requires coordinated cardio-obstetric care. During pregnancy, treatment includes loop diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers such as metoprolol, vasodilators considered safe in pregnancy, digoxin when needed, sodium restriction, and anticoagulation for severe LV dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, ventricular thrombus, or embolism. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided during pregnancy but may be used postpartum when compatible with lactation and maternal priorities. Delivery timing is individualized: obstetric indications guide stable patients, whereas refractory heart failure, shock, or fetal compromise may require urgent delivery in a tertiary center.

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion, is the most disease-specific therapy studied. A South African pilot trial and a German multicenter randomized study suggested improved LVEF recovery when bromocriptine was added to standard heart-failure therapy, particularly in severe PPCM [24,25]. Because bromocriptine suppresses lactation and may increase thrombotic risk, its use requires shared decision-making and concurrent anticoagulation. Contemporary cohorts treated with standard heart-failure therapy, and sometimes bromocriptine, demonstrate substantial recovery but persistent late relapse risk, supporting prolonged follow-up [26]. Women with LVEF ≤35% are at risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias; wearable defibrillators may bridge the early recovery period before considering implantable cardioverter-defibrillators [27].

Counseling about subsequent pregnancy is essential. Recurrence and deterioration are strongly related to preconception LVEF; persistent LV dysfunction confers high maternal risk and pregnancy is generally discouraged [28]. Even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur, so women should receive preconception evaluation, medication optimization, and surveillance with echocardiography during and after pregnancy [29]. Long-acting reversible contraception is usually preferred until recovery and counseling are complete. Guideline recommendations increasingly emphasize multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric teams, rapid recognition, individualized delivery planning, postpartum optimization of guideline-directed therapy, and culturally sensitive counseling about breastfeeding and future pregnancy [30].
